Binding the Strong Man
BYND-ing thuh STRAWNG man
noun phrase
From Greek deō (G1210, to bind) and ho ischuros (G2478, the strong one); Christ's parable of binding the strong man before spoiling his house (Matt 12:29; Mark 3:27).

📖 Biblical Definition

Binding the strong man is the Lord Jesus' own parabolic explanation of His authority over Satan, given in answer to the blasphemous charge that He cast out devils by Beelzebub. Christ asks, 'how can one enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? and then he will spoil his house' (Matt 12:29). The strong man is Satan; his house is his dominion over fallen men; his goods are the souls held captive at his will. The fact that Christ casts out demons is proof that the stronger has come upon the strong, has overpowered him, taken from him all his armor wherein he trusted, and divided his spoils (Luke 11:21-22). This is the inauguration of the kingdom of God in power. The Reformed faith confesses that at the cross and in His whole earthly ministry, Christ decisively bound the strong man, leading captivity captive and spoiling principalities and powers, making a show of them openly. The binding is not the final imprisonment of the last day but the present, real, conquering authority by which the gospel now plunders Satan's kingdom, calling the elect out of darkness into light. Every conversion is a spoiling of the strong man's house. Christ alone is the stronger man, and His victory is the ground of the believer's deliverance from the power of darkness and translation into the kingdom of God's dear Son.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christ's parable that He overpowers Satan, the strong man, and plunders his house, signifying the kingdom of God breaking in.

BINDING THE STRONG MAN, noun phrase. From Greek deō (G1210) and ho ischuros (G2478); Christ's parable of overpowering Satan before spoiling his house.

Spoken in answer to the charge that He cast out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of the devils.

The strong man is Satan; the house his dominion; the goods the souls held captive at his will.

As it is written, 'No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man; and then he will spoil his house' (Mark 3:27).

The casting out of demons proves the stronger has come, the inauguration of the kingdom of God in power.

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 12:29 — "Or else how can one enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? and then he will spoil his house."

Mar 3:27 — "No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man; and then he will spoil his house."

Luk 11:22 — "But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils."

Col 2:15 — "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The parable is sometimes wrenched into a method for human spiritual-warfare techniques, when its sole point is the unique conquering authority of Christ.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse is rather a practical one: turning 'binding the strong man' into a formula or technique by which believers rebuke and bind Satan through repeated verbal commands. The text gives no such warrant; the one who binds the strong man is Christ Himself, the stronger man, and the parable is about His unique victory, not a human method.

The principle to recover is that the kingdom of God came in power when the Son of God overpowered Satan, took his armor, and divided his spoils. The believer's deliverance rests entirely upon Christ's accomplished triumph at Calvary, where He spoiled principalities and powers openly. We do not bind Satan; we proclaim the One who already has, and every conversion is a soul plundered from the strong man's house.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek deō (G1210) and ho ischuros (G2478) frame Christ's parable of binding Satan and spoiling his goods.

expand to see more

Greek deō (G1210) — to bind, to tie fast, the act of overpowering the strong man

Greek ischuros (G2478) — strong, mighty; the strong man who is Satan

Greek ischuroteros (G2478 comparative) — stronger; Christ, the stronger who overcomes

Greek diarpazō (G1283) — to plunder, to spoil the goods of the house

Christ's exorcisms prove the kingdom of God is present and the strong man already bound

Usage

"Christ alone binds the strong man; every conversion spoils Satan's house."

"The casting out of demons proved the stronger man had come upon the strong."

"Binding the strong man is the inauguration of the kingdom, not a technique for men to repeat."
